items.prompt: A matrix has rows (1, 2) and (2, 1). What is its larger eigenvalue?
items.hint: Start with the trace and the determinant of the matrix, then put them into λ = (tr ± √(tr² − 4 det)) / 2.
items.explain: From the trace and determinant, the two roots of the quadratic are the eigenvalues. The larger one is {answer}.

items.prompt: A quarter turn has rows (0, −1) and (1, 0). What is tr² − 4 det for it?
items.hint: Add the two diagonal entries to get the trace. For the determinant, take ad − bc.
items.explain: tr² − 4 det is {answer}. It is negative, so a quarter turn has no real eigenvalues: no real arrow keeps its line.

items.prompt: You push on a rubber sheet. One drawn line stays on itself as a line, with points sliding along it, while all other lines tilt. What do the arrows along that line form?

choices.why: An arrow along a line that stays on itself comes out along the same line, only stretched or flipped: that is an eigenvector.
A rotation turns arrows; an eigenvector is an arrow that is not turned.
The zero vector has no direction and is excluded; the arrows along the line are not zero.

items.prompt: Before you continue, predict: if A − λI had an inverse, which v would satisfy (A − λI) v = 0?
items.reasoning: Only the zero vector, since a matrix with an inverse sends nothing else to zero. An eigenvector must not be zero, so A − λI must have no inverse, and so its determinant is 0.

items.prompt: In your own words: why can a rotation by 60° not have a real eigenvector?
items.model: A rotation by 60° turns every arrow by 60°, so no arrow stays on its own line. In numbers, tr² − 4 det is negative for it, so the quadratic that gives λ has no real solution.
